assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, followed by the 2017 association of a neutrino with the blazar TXS 0506+056, opened a new observational window onto cosmic-ray accelerators. This is a detector-driven discovery of the kind I value: a cubic-kilometre instrument in Antarctic ice that took decades of calibration and background control to make credible.
assessment.attribution: Halzen was the intellectual driver of the IceCube concept and Karle is credited alongside him for the detector's construction and delivery. IceCube is a very large collaboration and AMANDA, Baikal and other precursors matter, so a one-to-two person prize is a simplification. I judge the two names supportable but not beyond debate.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux has been confirmed repeatedly across analysis channels, and the Galactic-plane and NGC 1068 results strengthen the picture. Source identification is still developing, but the discovery of the neutrino flux itself is mature and timely.
uncertainties: Whether the credit should include other founders or collaboration leaders beyond the two supplied names.
The TXS 0506+056 source association is statistically modest; the prize case should rest on the diffuse flux.
I have not independently verified the exact significances or the order of the key papers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* are a direct, visually compelling test of strong-field gravity and black-hole physics. They are the product of a global very-long-baseline interferometry array, with demanding calibration, imaging and systematics control. I weigh that measurement craft heavily.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed imaging the shadow, Doeleman built and led the mm-VLBI effort and the EHT collaboration, and Zensus led the collaboration's organisation and the Bonn side. The collaboration has hundreds of members, and the roles of the many imaging and instrument contributors make a three-person prize contestable.
assessment.maturity: Two independent targets and multi-epoch M87* images exist, with polarisation results added. The interpretation depends on modelling choices and image-reconstruction methods, but recognition is arguably timely given the work's clarity and public impact.
uncertainties: Disputed or under-weighted credit for imaging-algorithm and instrument leaders beyond the three names.
Residual model dependence in inferring the shadow size and spin.
Whether the committee sees sufficient independent confirmation beyond the single collaboration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background from pulsar timing arrays opens a band complementary to LIGO, probably tied to supermassive black-hole binaries. It rests on years of precision timing, a prime example of patient instrumentation and systematics work.
assessment.attribution: Several PTA collaborations (NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, CPTA, InPTA) reported evidence in 2023, so credit is spread across them. Manchester and Kramer are long-standing leaders of Parkes and European timing efforts, and McLaughlin of NANOGrav. Which three names best represent the decisive contribution is unclear.
assessment.maturity: The Hellings-Downs correlation signal is only at the roughly 2 to 4 sigma level in individual datasets, and the astrophysical origin is unsettled. The case looks somewhat premature without a firmer detection.
uncertainties: Significance remains short of a definitive discovery.
Interpretation (supermassive black-hole binaries versus new physics) is unresolved.
Attribution is spread across five or more collaborations, and the supplied names may not reflect it fairly.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with its magic-wavelength trapping idea and demonstration at 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, redefined precision timekeeping and enables tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. It is an instrument-level advance with clear lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye built the leading demonstrations and drove the performance records. Credit is clean and a two-person prize is natural, though the Hall-Hänsch frequency-comb and ion-clock lineages are already or separately recognised.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups have confirmed the approach and a redefinition of the second is under discussion. It is mature, and it could be seen as timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior prizes for frequency combs and ion clocks may weigh against it.
Others, such as the Lemonde, Takamoto or Boyd contributions, could be argued as decisive.
Outside my own expertise in AMO physics; I would rely on colleagues for the details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon microstrip and hybrid pixel detectors underpin vertex tracking in nearly every modern collider experiment and in imaging far beyond particle physics. This is a transformative instrumentation invention, and as a detector builder I believe the field has been under-recognised relative to its impact.
assessment.attribution: Kemmer's planar process, Parker's microstrip work, and Heijne's hybrid-pixel development are each decisive for different parts of the technology. The compound nature of the discovery makes a clean three-person split hard, and other pixel pioneers (such as Campbell and Snoeys) could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of use in LEP, LHC, and light sources, so recognition is long overdue.
uncertainties: Credit allocation between strips and pixels is contested.
The committee has seldom awarded pure detector development unless tied to a discovery.
I have not verified the precise priority dates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light, proposed for interferometers by Caves and demonstrated in nonclassical states by Kimble's group, now improves the sensitivity of LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 in routine operation. It is an example of quantum optics turned into a working precision instrument.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the theoretical proposal, Kimble the first experimental squeezing, and Schnabel the GEO600 and later gravitational-wave implementation. Other contributors, including Slusher, Walls, Vahlbruch and the LIGO squeezing team, complicate the allocation.
assessment.maturity: Squeezed-light injection is now operational in all the major detectors, which is strong confirmation of the technique. The recognition appears timely.
uncertainties: The 2012 Nobel and the 2017 LIGO prize may reduce appetite for further quantum-optics or gravitational-wave awards.
Experimental priority among the early squeezing groups is disputed.
Quantum optics lies outside my core expertise.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The mapping of CMB acoustic peaks (WMAP, with earlier ground and balloon work) fixed the cosmological parameters to percent level and established precision cosmology. It is a very high-impact measurement made through exacting instrument and systematics control.
assessment.attribution: Bennett led WMAP, Spergel did the cosmological parameter analysis, and Page was a principal instrument designer. Puget (Planck), Sunyaev and other teams complicate the picture. Selection of three from five credited names is difficult, and the Planck and BOOMERanG contributions are legitimate competitors.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by Planck and many ground experiments; fully mature. However, the CMB has been recognised in 1978 and 2006, and 2019 for cosmology, so the committee may see this as a third or fourth recognition of the field.
uncertainties: Strong overlap with the 2006 Nobel for CMB anisotropy and blackbody spectrum.
Competing credit for Planck, BOOMERanG and ground-based experiments.
Whether the committee judges the acoustic-peak mapping as a distinct discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: X-ray free-electron lasers based on SASE have given femtosecond, coherent X-ray pulses and opened up ultrafast structural science in physics, chemistry and biology. The machine physics is demanding, and the impact is broad and durable.
assessment.attribution: Pellegrini's SASE theory and proposals, Rossbach's TESLA test facility and FLASH work, and Ishikawa's SACLA are significant. Other figures, such as Bonifacio, Kondratenko, Saldin, Emma and Huang, are arguably decisive too, so the supplied names may not capture all the decisive credit.
assessment.maturity: Multiple facilities (LCLS, SACLA, European XFEL, FLASH) confirm the concept, so it is mature. The prize case is tied to the science done with the instrument as much as the invention.
uncertainties: Priority and credit in the SASE concept are spread across many accelerator physicists.
The prize might fit chemistry or be seen as accelerator technology.
Outside my direct expertise; I would defer to accelerator specialists.
